title: Given coin denominations and a total amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make that amount, where each denomination can be used unlimited times. Return minus one if it cannot be made. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack minimization DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Minimum Coin Change (Fewest Coins to Make an Amount)

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Coin Change is the minimization variant of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. We fill an array where each slot holds the fewest coins to form that amount, initialized to an impossible-high sentinel, and for each amount we try every coin and take the best. If the final slot is still the sentinel the amount is unreachable. Time is amount times denominations and space is amount.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants its cash dispenser to hand out a requested amount using as few notes as possible, which keeps the dispenser efficient and the customer's wallet tidy. Minimum Coin Change computes that fewest-note count.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill each amount with the fewest coins by trying every denomination and taking one plus the best remainder.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Coin Change is the minimization variant of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. We fill an array where each slot holds the fewest coins to form that amount, initialized to an impossible-high sentinel, and for each amount we try every coin and take the best. If the final slot is still the sentinel the amount is unreachable. Time is amount times denominations and space is amount.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants its cash dispenser to hand out a requested amount using as few notes as possible, which keeps the dispenser efficient and the customer's wallet tidy. Minimum Coin Change computes that fewest-note count.

**One line to remember:** Fill each amount with the fewest coins by trying every denomination and taking one plus the best remainder.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep an array `dp[a]` meaning the fewest coins to form amount `a`. We initialize every slot to a sentinel larger than any real answer, such as amount plus one, and set `dp[0] = 0` because zero needs no coins.

For each amount from one to the target we try each coin that fits and take `dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], 1 + dp[a - coin])`, meaning one coin of that denomination plus the best way to make the remainder. A concrete step: to make amount six with a coin of value four, consider one coin plus the fewest coins for amount two. After filling, if `dp[amount]` still holds the sentinel the amount cannot be formed and we return minus one. Senior nuance: this is a minimization over an unbounded supply, so the amount loop can be outer and the coin loop inner without worrying about combination versus permutation, because we are taking a minimum rather than counting; the greedy largest-coin-first approach can fail for arbitrary denominations, which is why the DP is necessary.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants its cash dispensers to use the fewest notes possible when dispensing a requested amount, which reduces mechanical wear and gives the customer fewer notes to handle. A naive largest-note-first greedy can fail for some denomination sets, dispensing more notes than necessary or getting stuck. This is exactly how Minimum Coin Change works: a DP that always finds the true minimum.

The code defines a `MinNotesService` exposing `minCoins(denominations, amount)` returning the fewest notes, or minus one if impossible. A `Demo` runs it over note denominations and an amount and logs the fewest-note count.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is note denominations 1, 3, 5 and an amount of seven.

Step 1 — We create an array of length eight filled with the sentinel eight, then set dp[0] to zero. Only amount zero has a known fewest-note count.

Step 2 — For amount one, only note one fits, so dp[1] becomes one plus dp[0] equals one. For amount two, dp[2] becomes one plus dp[1] equals two.

Step 3 — For amount three, note one gives one plus dp[2] equals three, and note three gives one plus dp[0] equals one, so dp[3] is one. For amount four, note one gives one plus dp[3] equals two, note three gives one plus dp[1] equals two, so dp[4] is two.

Step 4 — For amount five, note five gives one plus dp[0] equals one, so dp[5] is one. For amount six, note three gives one plus dp[3] equals two, so dp[6] is two.

Step 5 — For amount seven, note one gives one plus dp[6] equals three, note three gives one plus dp[4] equals three, note five gives one plus dp[2] equals three, so dp[7] is two using a five and... checking, note five then two more via two notes gives three, but note three plus note three plus note one is three notes; the true minimum is dp[7] equal to three? Recomputing: dp[7] is the minimum over note one giving one plus dp[6] equals three, note three giving one plus dp[4] equals three, note five giving one plus dp[2] equals three. So the fewest notes for seven is three, for example five plus one plus one, or three plus three plus one. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:21:00 PM com.bank.minnotes.service.MinNotesService minCoins
INFO: Fewest notes for 7 = 3
Oct 27, 2026 9:21:00 PM com.bank.minnotes.MinNotesApplication main
INFO: Fewest notes to dispense 7: 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Coin Change is the minimization flavour of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. I keep an array where each slot stores the fewest coins needed to form that amount, and I initialize every slot to a sentinel larger than any possible real answer, except the amount zero which needs zero coins. This sentinel lets me distinguish an amount that genuinely cannot be formed from one that simply needs many coins.

For each amount I try every denomination that fits and take the minimum of the current value and one plus the fewest coins for the remaining amount after using that denomination. Because the supply is unlimited and I am taking a minimum rather than counting, I do not have to worry about the combination-versus-permutation loop-order subtlety that the counting version has. After filling the table, if the target slot still holds the sentinel I return minus one. I always reach for the DP rather than a greedy largest-coin-first rule, because greedy can fail for arbitrary denomination sets.

At the National Bank of India I used this so cash dispensers handed out a requested amount using the fewest notes, reducing mechanical wear and giving customers fewer notes to carry. I ran the minimization DP with a sentinel initialization and returned minus one when an amount could not be formed from the available denominations. Explaining the sentinel, the one-plus-best-remainder recurrence, and why greedy is unsafe for general denominations is what shows an interviewer I understand the minimization form of Unbounded Knapsack.
